entries.clue: With regard to getting answers, new year, new you? (11)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is the slogan rather than a synonym: what 'new year, new you' asks for is exactly the plural promises the answer names.

blocks.note: re is the 'with regard to' printed at the head of a memo
the answers to a puzzle or a problem are its solutions, and the plural is kept

annotation.surface: A note about getting answers, and the promise of a reinvented self for the new year.
annotation.walkthrough: Re is the memo heading, printed above every reply anyone ever sent, and it is the only convention here. The definition is the January slogan rather than a dictionary synonym — what people promise themselves on the first of the month.
annotation.definitionFit: New Year's resolutions are the promises made on 1 January to become a better version of yourself, which is all 'new year, new you' means.

entries.clue: Maybe having a facelift? Surprising! (7,8)

blocks.note: the surgical sense taken literally, the brow lifted by a knife; 'maybe' admits this is one such operation among several
the figurative sense: what startles a room sends the brows up by themselves

annotation.surface: Someone has had work done, and the result is a shock.
annotation.walkthrough: Both readings are the same gesture, one performed by a surgeon and one by surprise. 'Maybe' is doing proper work: a facelift is only one of the procedures that lifts a brow, so the first definition is by example.
annotation.definitionFit: A facelift physically lifts the brows, and news that raises eyebrows is news people find surprising — the same movement, once with a scalpel and once without.

entries.clue: Film genre capturing hearts of muscly Brits – uplifting anime (3-2)

indicatorNotes.hearts of: The heart of a word is what sits at its very centre, so each word named gives up its middle letter or letters and nothing else.

blocks.note: the middle two of its six letters
the third of five letters
the fifth of nine letters
the third of five letters

annotation.surface: A film genre that has won over beefy Britons, along with feel-good Japanese animation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Uplifting' is the trap: in a down clue it reads as an instruction to turn letters upwards, and here it is fodder like the three words around it. Four words are quarried, one after another.
annotation.definitionFit: Sci-fi is the everyday abbreviation of science fiction, one of the standard genres a film gets shelved under.

entries.clue: Confusing Australian/American slang for Italian dish (7)

indicatorNotes.Confusing: Something confusing cannot be taken at face value, and letters described that way are not in the order they will end up in.

blocks.note: a is the standard single letter for each of those nationalities, and the clue asks for both
five letters for the pile, taken for their spelling rather than their sense

annotation.surface: Australian and American slang collide over the name of an Italian dish.
annotation.walkthrough: The dish is spelt with a final A in America and with an E in Britain, so 'American' does two jobs: a letter for the pile and a hint at which ending the grid wants.
annotation.definitionFit: Lasagna is the baked dish of flat pasta sheets layered with sauce and cheese, Italian by origin and spelt here the American way.

entries.clue: Stomp over sheep pelt, mangled on the outside (7)

indicatorNotes.mangled: Something mangled has been crushed out of its proper shape, and letters in that state do not stay in the order given.
indicatorNotes.on the outside: What is on the outside surrounds what is within, so these letters part and take the other piece between them.

blocks.note: the four letters of the hide in a new order, ready to close on something
a ram is the male sheep

annotation.surface: Walking heavily over a sheepskin that is chewed up round its edges.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pelt' is the fleece of the picture and a pile of letters in the wordplay. 'On the outside' says where the sheep goes rather than describing the damage done to the hide.
annotation.definitionFit: To trample something is to stomp on it repeatedly, and both verbs describe feet doing the damage.

entries.clue: Best available public transport capsized (8)

indicatorNotes.capsized: A capsized boat has turned right over, so the letters in front of the word are read from their far end.

blocks.note: a book that is out is available, on sale
trams are public transport, and the plural is the five letters wanted

annotation.surface: The finest public transport on offer has turned over in the water.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Best available public transport' reads as a single phrase and is a definition plus two pieces. 'Best' is the verb: to best someone is to get the better of them.
annotation.definitionFit: To outsmart a rival is to best them — both verbs mean beating someone by cleverness rather than by force.

entries.clue: Tendency to keep away from stall with salmon, perhaps, on Scottish headland (15)

indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry one thing sits on another by being higher in the column, so the piece in front of this word takes the earlier cells.

blocks.note: a market stall is a stand
a stall with salmon on it is a stall of fish, which is the sense of 'with' being used
salmon is one fish among many, which is what 'perhaps' signals
a ness is a headland, and Scotland's coastline is full of them

annotation.surface: A fish stall set up on a Scottish promontory.
annotation.walkthrough: Ness is the northern word for a headland, which is why so much of the Scottish map ends in it. The small word doing the real work is 'with': a stall with salmon on it is a stall of fish.
annotation.definitionFit: Standoffishness is the habit of keeping people at arm's length — the noun for a tendency to keep away rather than for any single act.

entries.clue: Book of the Bible supporting origins of one decidedly deadly Bond villain (6)

indicatorNotes.supporting: In a down entry whatever supports something else sits underneath it, so this piece takes the lower cells.
indicatorNotes.origins of: The origin of a word is the letter it starts from, so each of the words that follow gives up its first letter.

blocks.note: the opening letters of the three words, in the order they come
Job is the Old Testament book about the man who loses everything and keeps his faith

annotation.surface: Scripture propping up the beginnings of a lethal film henchman.
annotation.walkthrough: The villain is Goldfinger's bowler-hatted chauffeur, who kills people with the brim of his hat. 'Supporting' is positional rather than approving: in a down clue the scripture sits underneath.
annotation.definitionFit: Oddjob is Goldfinger's silent bodyguard, one of the best known of all the villains in the Bond films.

entries.clue: Second time around part of forest road (6)

indicatorNotes.around: Something that goes around a thing closes on it from both sides, so the letters already assembled part to let the next piece in.

blocks.note: s is the standard single letter for second
t is the standard single letter for time
one tree is a part of a forest

annotation.surface: The second time around, on a road through part of a forest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Part of forest' looks like an instruction to dig a hidden run out of the words beside it, and it is a plain definition instead. 'Second time around' is the idiom the surface leans on.
annotation.definitionFit: A street is a road with buildings along it, the town version of the same thing.

entries.clue: Raised platform that is shaped at the front for flowers (7)

indicatorNotes.at the front: At the front of a word is where it begins, so only its opening letter is taken.

blocks.note: a dais is the raised platform a speaker stands on
i.e. is id est, Latin for 'that is'
the first letter of the word 'shaped'

annotation.surface: A platform built up at one end and decorated with flowers.
annotation.walkthrough: I.e. is one of the handful of two-letter abbreviations a setter drops in unannounced, and 'that is' is its full form rather than a pointer to the definition. The platform is the speaker's kind.
annotation.definitionFit: Daisies are the small white-and-yellow flowers of any lawn, and the plural definition matches the plural answer.

entries.clue: Draw, roughly, cat and rat with trucker’s cap (7)

indicatorNotes.roughly: Something done roughly is done without care for where things end up, so these letters will not stay in the order given.
indicatorNotes.cap: A cap goes on the head, and the head of a word is the letter it starts with, so that letter alone is taken.

blocks.note: three letters for the pile, taken for their spelling
three more, again as they are spelt
the first letter of the word 'trucker'

annotation.surface: A quick sketch of a cat and a rat wearing a trucker's cap.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Draw, roughly' reads as one instruction to an artist, and the comma is all that separates the definition from the shuffle. A trucker's cap is the mesh-backed baseball sort.
annotation.definitionFit: To attract someone is to draw them in — both verbs take the same object and mean pulling something towards you.

entries.clue: Couple with Pingu, randomly, getting a membership (7,2)

indicatorNotes.randomly: What is done randomly is done in no particular order, so the letters beside it are not to be read as they are given.

blocks.note: to couple two things is to join them
the five letters of the cartoon penguin's name, reordered

annotation.surface: A couple sign up for something in the company of a cartoon penguin.
annotation.walkthrough: Pingu is the claymation penguin of the children's television series, and his name is here for its letters alone. 'Couple' is the verb rather than the pair of people the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: Joining up is what you do to acquire a membership, whether of a gym, a union or the army.

entries.clue: Fly film I’d generally disregarded somewhat (5)

indicatorNotes.somewhat: Somewhat means partly rather than wholly, so only some of the letters in front are wanted — a run of them, in the order they come.

blocks.note: five consecutive letters, starting on the last letter of the first word
the verb the surface needs for a film one had ignored, and it asks for no letters

annotation.surface: A film the speaker had never much bothered with.
annotation.walkthrough: The run begins on the last letter of the first word and ends two into the third, crossing two gaps — the hardest kind to spot. The insect meant is the tiny biting one that swarms on Scottish summer evenings.
annotation.definitionFit: A midge is a very small two-winged fly, so 'fly' is simply the family it belongs to.

entries.clue: BA guards emptied out luggage (4)

indicatorNotes.emptied out: A thing emptied out keeps only its shell, so the word beside it loses its middle and leaves the letters at its two ends.

blocks.note: the clue's own two letters, British Airways in the surface, taken as they stand
the first and last letters of the word, with everything between them gone

annotation.surface: Airline security staff turn a suitcase inside out.
annotation.walkthrough: BA is British Airways, and its letters go in exactly as the clue prints them, with no synonym required. The emptying is done to the word 'guards', not to the luggage of the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: Bags are what you check in and collect off the belt, and luggage is the collective word for the same things.

entries.clue: Fake port I’m crazy to sell on for more (4,6)

indicatorNotes.crazy: Something crazy has lost its proper order, and letters called crazy will not be read in the order they are given.

blocks.note: ten letters for the pile, the apostrophe carrying no weight

annotation.surface: Someone is mad enough to buy counterfeit port and pass it on at a markup.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fake port' is the thing the surface asks you to picture, and both its words are fodder. 'I'm crazy to' reads as regret and is the shuffling instruction, with the setter's own I counted into the pile.
annotation.definitionFit: Selling something on for more than you paid for it is the plainest way there is to make a profit.

entries.clue: A year besieged by compliments leads to increase in wages in USA (3,5)

indicatorNotes.besieged by: A besieged town has the enemy all round it, so the letters in front go inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: compliments are praise, and the word opens up after its first letter
the clue's own word, taken as it stands
y is the standard single letter for year

annotation.surface: A year of nothing but compliments ends in more money.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In USA' is doing real work: the British name for the same thing is a different word, and the grid wants the American one. What the compliments surround is an article and a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A pay raise is the American name for the increase in wages that a British worker would call a pay rise.

entries.clue: Good weather in the new year? Time for some mocktails! (3,7)

blocks.note: weather with no rain in it, which in Britain counts as good
the month the new year opens with

annotation.surface: Rain-free days at the start of the year, and a round of alcohol-free drinks.
annotation.walkthrough: The pun sits on the weather word: rainless and teetotal are two quite different senses of it, and the clue offers the first to hide the second. Mocktails are cocktails with the spirits left out.
annotation.definitionFit: Dry January is the campaign of giving up alcohol for the whole month, which is when the mocktails come out.

entries.clue: Stop – hiding in Lourdes is trespassing (6)

indicatorNotes.hiding in: Something hiding in a place is inside it and out of sight, so the letters wanted sit unbroken within the words that follow.

blocks.note: six consecutive letters, starting inside the first word and running on through the second

annotation.surface: Sheltering in a pilgrimage town turns out to be against the law.
annotation.walkthrough: The hiding place crosses two word breaks, which is where the eye is least likely to look. Lourdes is the French pilgrimage town where the sick go to bathe in the spring water.
annotation.definitionFit: To desist is to stop doing what you are doing, the formal verb a court order uses in 'cease and desist'.

entries.clue: Honourable puritan invested in long life (7)

indicatorNotes.invested in: To be invested in a thing is to be put into it, so the word before this goes inside the letters that follow.

blocks.note: UHT is ultra heat treated, the label on the long-life milk that keeps for months without a fridge
a prig is a self-righteous moraliser

annotation.surface: A strait-laced moralist with money in a long-life product.
annotation.walkthrough: UHT is stamped on the cartons of long-life milk in every British supermarket — ultra heat treated, so it survives unopened in a cupboard. 'Invested' belongs to the money of the surface and means inserted.
annotation.definitionFit: An upright citizen is honourable — straight in their dealings, the posture word borrowed to describe a character.

entries.clue: Volatile AI rated broadcast (7)

indicatorNotes.Volatile: A volatile substance will not hold still, and letters described that way will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: seven letters for the pile, taken for their spelling rather than their sense

annotation.surface: An unstable artificial intelligence gets reviewed on air.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is the word that wants to be the shuffling instruction, and it is the definition instead — sitting at the end of the clue, where an anagram signal so often does.
annotation.definitionFit: To radiate heat or confidence is to send it out in all directions, which is what a transmitter does when it broadcasts.

entries.clue: Setter becoming single – time to lose weight? (4)

indicatorNotes.becoming single: Becoming single asks for the singular of the word in front of it, which is spelt differently from the plural.

blocks.note: this puzzle is signed Dice, and one of a pair of dice is a die
t is the standard single letter for time

annotation.surface: Newly on their own, someone decides it is time to shed a few pounds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Setter' is the crossword writer naming himself, and this one signs as Dice, so it is his own name that has to be made singular. In other clues a setter would be the dog.
annotation.definitionFit: To diet is to eat sparingly in order to lose weight, so the definition names the purpose the verb exists for.

entries.clue: Catching every other St Ives shoot – we watch it on the box (2,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer rather than replacing it — the thing we watch on the box — and the 'we' in front of it is also the last word the wordplay counts through.

indicatorNotes.Catching every other: Catching every other one means taking the second, the fourth, the sixth and so on, and letting the ones between them go.

blocks.note: the even-numbered letters of the run, read in the order they come

annotation.surface: Only every second take from a Cornish location shoot makes it to our screens.
annotation.walkthrough: The count runs on past the dash and into the definition's first word, which is why the harvest looks a letter short. St Ives is the Cornish harbour town the painters colonised.
annotation.definitionFit: 'The box' is the British name for the television set, and a TV show is what people sit down to watch on it.

entries.clue: Senior picking up award for not drinking (5)

indicatorNotes.picking up: To pick something up is to take it in and carry it, so what follows is gathered inside the letters in front.

blocks.note: Sr is how a name is shortened when father and son share it
the OBE is the Order of the British Empire, one of the honours the monarch hands out twice a year

annotation.surface: An elderly man collects a medal for staying off the drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The honours list gives the setter three ready letters and the shortening for the older of two men gives two more. 'Picking up' is what you do at the palace, and it is also the instruction to enclose.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone sober is not drinking — either not drunk at this moment or off alcohol altogether.

entries.clue: They might indicate sex workers guided Conservative groups, according to Spooner (3,6)

indicatorNotes.according to Spooner: Spooner was the Oxford don remembered for swapping the opening sounds of two words, and a clue in his name asks you to do the same.

blocks.note: to guide is to lead, and the Conservative side of politics is the right, whose factions are rights; trading the two opening sounds spells it the other way

annotation.surface: Sex workers are alleged to have steered groups of Conservatives.
annotation.walkthrough: The Reverend Spooner's trick is to trade the opening sounds of two words, so the clue hands you the phrase the wrong way round and leaves you to switch it back. The 'right' wanted is the political one.
annotation.definitionFit: A red light in a window has marked a brothel for well over a century, and a red-light district is where sex workers work.

entries.clue: Bury playwright, Harold, without his head? (5)

indicatorNotes.without: Without a thing means it is not there, so whatever the clue names next is taken away from the letters in front.

blocks.note: Harold Pinter, the British playwright of The Caretaker and The Birthday Party
the head of a name is the letter it starts with, and this is the one that goes

annotation.surface: A macabre suggestion about the burial of a famous dramatist.
annotation.walkthrough: Pinter won the Nobel for plays full of menacing pauses, and his surname is exactly one letter longer than the grid has room for. The question mark is the setter owning up to a grisly picture.
annotation.definitionFit: To inter a body is to bury it, the formal verb used of funerals and of what a churchyard does.

entries.clue: Special little moment with man having a puff (7)

blocks.note: s is the standard single letter for special
a mo is a moment cut short
the king is one of the men on a chessboard

annotation.surface: A brief special occasion shared with a man out for a cigarette.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Man' is a chessboard piece rather than a person, one of the swaps a setter expects you to carry. 'Half a mo' is still everyday British for wait a second, and that is the moment being shortened.
annotation.definitionFit: Having a puff is having a smoke: the gerund matches, and both name the act of drawing on a cigarette.

entries.clue: Rate Doc’s unusual 20s style (3,4)

indicatorNotes.unusual: What is unusual is not as it normally comes, so these letters are not in their normal order.

blocks.note: seven letters for the pile, the apostrophe-s reading as 'is' in the surface

annotation.surface: A doctor's odd taste in nineteen-twenties furnishings is being judged.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rate Doc's unusual' reads as a verdict on a person and is a pile of letters plus its instruction. The style meant is the geometric one of the Chrysler Building and the old Odeon cinemas.
annotation.definitionFit: Art Deco is the sleek geometric style of the 1920s and 30s — sunbursts, chrome and zigzags — so a decade names it.

entries.clue: Go in street, catch bottoms of exuberant reckless lovers (11)

indicatorNotes.in: In names the place a thing goes into, so the piece before it is set inside the word that follows.
indicatorNotes.bottoms of: The bottom of a word is where it finishes, so each of the words named gives up its final letter.

blocks.note: st is the standard shortening of street, as on any address
a wee is the British nursery word for a pee, and 'go' is the polite way of asking for the same thing
to catch what someone said is to hear it — 'I didn't catch that'
the final letter of each of the two words

annotation.surface: Out in the road, grabbing at the backsides of a giddy pair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go' is the euphemism a parent uses before a car journey, and it is three letters long. 'Catch' looks like another instruction to enclose and is a plain synonym for hearing.
annotation.definitionFit: Sweethearts are lovers — the old-fashioned word for a courting pair, and plural to match the definition.
